name: Neckmaxxing / neck training

lead: Neckmaxxing is training the neck muscles to make the neck thicker, which proponents say gives a more masculine, dominant look and better balance between the head, jaw and body. It is described on looksmax.org as a softmaxx.

Neck exercises load the muscles around the cervical spine, with the sternocleidomastoid named in forum guides as the muscle that thickens the neck from the front. Forum posts offer ratio targets, such as neck width to bigonial (jaw) width near 1:1 or a neck-to-height ratio near 1.35, and say a wider neck makes a narrow head and jaw look more in proportion. These are community conventions; no published study validates them and no clinical studies of neck training for appearance were found.

paras: People follow forum guides using neck curls, extensions and similar loaded movements added to a lifting routine, and track neck width with a tape. A thicker neck builds over months of consistent training.
Loaded neck exercises sit near the cervical spine, and one forum guide calls neck work one of the most dangerous softmaxxes. Gradual loading and careful form are the usual precautions in guides.

web.title: How to get a thicker neck - Healthline

angle.text: Neckmaxxers train the neck to make it thicker, which they say adds a masculine, dominant look and better face and frame proportions. A wider neck sits more in balance with the jaw and shoulders. Neck-to-jaw ratio targets circulate on forums, and no published study validates them.

lead: Neckmaxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of training the neck muscles to build a thicker, more defined neck. Practitioners say a wider neck gives the head and jaw a stronger frame, adds to a masculine, powerful look and balances a broad jaw or shoulders, and forum members describe it as one of the more visible changes available from lifting.[1][2][3]

Forum guides describe neck curls, extensions and side raises, sometimes with a towel or a weight plate, plus slow bodyweight variations that emphasise stretch.[3][4] Community posts give proportion targets: a neck-to-bigonial (jaw width) ratio of about 0.95 to 1, a neck matching the widest part of the face, and in one thread a neck width-to-height ratio near 1.35.[1][2] These are community conventions rather than published standards.

Outside looksmaxxing, neck strengthening is studied in sport and rehabilitation. A randomised trial in healthy women found that ten weeks of neck training increased the cross-sectional area of the neck muscles, with larger gains when resistance work was combined with proprioceptive exercises.[5] Consumer health writing also lists flexion, extension, lateral flexion and rotation exercises and says a muscular neck looks strong, especially when flexed.[6]

paras: Forum guides describe adding neck exercises such as curls and extensions to a lifting routine. One author calls the neck among the most dangerous yet rewarding softmaxxes and claims it could add about 0.5 PSL points.[2] PSL is a community rating scale for looks and is not a validated measure.

A thread titled as a guide lists the benefits as a thicker and stronger neck that can go with the physique, improved posture over time and what the author calls a 'high T' look; it demonstrates two exercises done with a towel over the head.[3] Replies in that thread suggest slow tempo and stretch can produce growth even without added weight.[3]

Posters compare necks to celebrity examples and discuss proportions with the head and jaw, saying that people with a small or narrow skull may already be proportional while those with a wide skull would need to build neck size.[1] A guide on the sternocleidomastoid describes keeping the neck 'packed' during curls.[2] Before and after posts show results of neck training alongside other changes.

Common questions on looksmax.org include how often to train, whether training one side more will leave the neck asymmetrical, and what to change when two months of training shows no results.[4][7] One thread title argues neck training is important for people who have a wider face and better jawline but still a thin neck.[8]

A ten-week randomised pilot trial in 26 healthy women reported neck muscle cross-sectional area increases in all three muscle groups measured, between 1.5 and 12.9 percent in a resistance-only group and 18.9 to 32.3 percent in a resistance plus proprioceptive group.[5] A randomised study of 180 women with chronic neck pain found neck strength rose most in a high-intensity isometric group, with gains continuing across 12 months.[9]

In sports medicine, a systematic review and Delphi consensus examined neck training to reduce head acceleration events in sport.[10] Healthline's guide to a thicker neck lists exercises and says a muscular neck looks strong, and that neck exercises can ease tension and help prevent injury.[6]

Health writing advises stopping any neck exercise that causes pain and moving slowly with good posture.[6] One looksmax.org thread title raises the possibility that neck training can cause sleep apnoea,[11] while Healthline notes that excess neck fat, rather than muscle, may raise sleep apnoea risk.[6]

No studies found of neck training for facial or physique appearance in the looksmaxxing sense. Related studies of neck training include a randomised pilot trial measuring neck muscle size after resistance and proprioceptive training,[5] a 12-month randomised study of strength training for chronic neck pain,[9] a Delphi consensus on neck training in sport[10] and trials of corticomotor effects of neck training.[12]

lore.intro: Neckmaxxing threads on looksmax.org mix anatomy, ratio targets, training guides and progress photos.[1][2][4]
